Direct 2-D aperture integration of the TE10 field with each plane's quadratic phase gives 22.6000 dBi.

archetypes.notes: WHAT MAKES A PYRAMIDAL HORN BUILDABLE. Each plane's flare, run back from the aperture, points at an apex: rho1 behind the aperture in the E-plane, rho2 in the H-plane. The optimum-gain proportions are b1 = sqrt(2 lambda rho1) and a1 = sqrt(3 lambda rho2), i.e. phase errors s = 1/4 and t = 3/8, and the gain then fixes the product rho1*rho2. What remains is the condition that the two flares meet the FEED WAVEGUIDE at the same axial length: rho1 (1 - b/b1) = rho2 (1 - a/a1). This spec used to set rho1 = rho2 - a single apex - which only fits a guide with the aperture's own aspect ratio, sqrt(3/2); every standard guide is about 2:1, and on WR-90 at 20 dBi the two flares reached the guide 15 mm apart. It also called its single rho a slant length while every formula used it as the axial one. With rho1 = chi lambda, the condition is a quartic in s = sqrt(chi): s^4 - (b/lambda/sqrt2) s^3 + (a/lambda) (P/sqrt3) s - P^2 = 0, P = G0/(4 pi eta_opt sqrt 6). The textbook procedure (Balanis, Ch. 13) reaches a degree-8 form of the same condition by writing the optimum proportions in SLANT lengths and sizing with an implied efficiency of 0.5105; by direct aperture integration that lands 0.04-0.19 dB below target at 20-25 dBi and 0.8 dB below at 15. Written in axial distances with the exact optimum efficiency, the gain is on target and the phase errors are exactly 1/4 and 3/8 - checked by 2-D aperture integration, and the flare-meeting condition by bisection on its unsquared form.

archetypes.name: E-plane sectoral horn (optimum)
archetypes.summary: Waveguide flared in the E plane only, with the directivity taken from Balanis's exact Fresnel-integral form rather than a pinned aperture efficiency.

parameters.name: flare relative to optimum
parameters.description: b1 divided by the optimum sqrt(2*lambda*rho); 1.0 is the maximum-gain flare

synthesis.notes: The optimum flare b1 = sqrt(2*lambda*rho) puts a quarter-wavelength of quadratic phase error at the aperture edge, which is where gain peaks. `flare` scales away from it.

b1/sqrt(2*lambda*rho); exactly 1 at the optimum, and equal to `flare`. Everything about the aperture efficiency depends on this one number and on nothing else - not on frequency, not on the absolute size.

analysis.notes: EXACT, from Balanis 13-19 rearranged: eta = (8/pi^2)*[C(q)^2 + S(q)^2]/q^2. The 8/pi^2 is the TE10 cosine taper across the unflared width; the Fresnel term is the quadratic phase across the flare. 0.64870 at the optimum, where this spec previously carried a hard-coded 0.65.
Balanis 13-19 as published, kept alongside as an independent route to the same number - it must equal the gain above.
s = b1^2/(8*lambda*rho), the quadratic phase error at the aperture edge. Exactly 0.25 at the optimum flare.

archetypes.name: Conical horn (optimum gain)
archetypes.summary: Circular waveguide flared into a cone, with the aperture efficiency integrated from the TE11 aperture field.

parameters.name: flare relative to the sqrt(3*lambda*L) rule

synthesis.notes: Quadratic phase error at the aperture rim, in wavelengths. It is exactly 0.375*flare^2, so the sqrt(3*lambda*L) rule puts it at 3/8 - and the efficiency depends on this number and nothing else.

analysis.notes: Integrated from the circular-guide TE11 aperture field with quadratic phase, then fitted over s in [0, 0.8]; worst error 0.0002. At zero phase error it gives 0.83683, the published TE11 circular-aperture value, which is the check that the integral is set up right. See the note on the 0.51 this spec used to pin.

SOLVED by aperture integration (otahub.num.horn_pattern: the circular guide TE11 field, quadratic phase, Huygens obliquity) and fitted as the half-power point U = D sin(theta_h) in edge phase error and 1/D^2 over D = 1.5-40 wavelengths: 0.20% worst on 207 patterns, 0.21% on 5 held out. HPBW = 2 asin(U/D), so the sine mapping is exact for small apertures. The flat 60 lambda/dm this spec carried is 7% narrow at the default flare (64.3) and grows fast after; it turns NaN below an aperture of 1.5 wavelengths, where the fit has no data, and past a phase error of 0.55, where the E-plane beam is collapsing - 82 lambda/dm at s = 0.55, 123 at 0.60, 156 at the 0.634 of a 1.3 flare.

SOLVED by aperture integration (otahub.num.horn_pattern: the circular guide TE11 field, quadratic phase, Huygens obliquity) and fitted as the half-power point U = D sin(theta_h) in edge phase error and 1/D^2 over D = 1.5-40 wavelengths: 0.48% worst on 207 patterns, 0.49% on 5 held out. HPBW = 2 asin(U/D), so the sine mapping is exact for small apertures. The flat 70 lambda/dm this spec carried is 8% narrow at the default flare (75.9); the H plane is the WIDER of the two because the TE11 field is tapered across it, and it holds up longer as the flare grows. It turns NaN below an aperture of 1.5 wavelengths, where the fit has no data, and past a phase error of 0.72, where the H-plane beam starts to collapse - 113 lambda/dm at 0.74, 157 at 0.78.

validity: aperture-field model with the unperturbed TE11 distribution and a quadratic phase across the flare; it ignores flare-edge diffraction and throat reflection
the exact spherical path difference is slightly SMALLER than the quadratic approximation, so this underestimates efficiency - by 0.2% at a 6 degree flare half-angle, 3% at 22 degrees
the efficiency fit covers s in [0, 0.8]; beyond that a degree-6 polynomial diverges rather than degrades
beamwidth figures are indicative and hold near the optimum flare only

known_cases.source: The sqrt(3*lambda*L) flare puts 3/8 of a wavelength at the rim, where the integrated efficiency is 0.53847. This spec used to pin 0.51, which is the efficiency at the TRUE maximum-gain flare (s = 0.3908, eta = 0.51760) - a different convention. Pinning one convention's efficiency while synthesising the other's aperture cost 0.24 dB.

Near the uniform-phase limit: a 0.1 flare leaves only 0.00375 wavelengths of edge phase error, where the efficiency is 0.836793 against the zero-phase value 0.836829 - the 0.836 quoted in the literature. A vanishing flare would test the limit more exactly but would describe a horn a fraction of a millimetre across, so this stops at a small aperture that is still a real antenna.
sqrt(3*lambda*L) = 164.26 mm at 10 GHz for a 300 mm slant

Over-flaring to 1.3x drives s to 0.6338 and the efficiency down to 0.21599 - less than half the optimum. A pinned efficiency cannot express this, and would have claimed the larger aperture was simply better.

archetypes.name: Corrugated (scalar) conical horn
archetypes.summary: Conical horn with lambda/4 corrugations, giving a symmetric HE11 balanced-hybrid pattern.

parameters.name: flare relative to the sqrt(3*lambda*L) rule

synthesis.notes: Quarter-wave corrugations present an anisotropic surface that forces the balanced hybrid HE11 mode - which is what makes the E and H patterns identical and the cross-polarisation low.

analysis.notes: Integrated from the balanced hybrid HE11 aperture field, which is a J0(2.405*rho/a) taper, with quadratic phase. At zero phase error it gives 0.69157 - the 0.69 quoted for corrugated horns, now derived rather than assumed. Fitted over s in [0, 0.8], worst error 0.0001.

SOLVED by aperture integration (otahub.num.horn_pattern: the balanced hybrid HE11 field, J0(2.405 r/a), quadratic phase, Huygens obliquity) and fitted as the half-power point U = D sin(theta_h) in edge phase error and 1/D^2 over D = 1.5-40 wavelengths: 0.06% worst on 207 patterns, 0.07% on 5 held out. HPBW = 2 asin(U/D), so the sine mapping is exact for small apertures. The flat 66 lambda/dm this spec carried was 13% narrow even with no phase error - a J0 taper to zero at the rim gives 75.7 - and 18% narrow at the default flare (80.2). It is still one figure for both planes, which is the point of the design. It turns NaN below an aperture of 1.5 wavelengths, where the fit has no data, and past a phase error of 0.8, where the fit stops at the edge of the efficiency fit's range.
INDICATIVE. A well-made corrugated horn reaches -30 dB or better over a wide band; the balanced hybrid condition is what suppresses it, and this spec does not compute the residual.

Both efficiencies integrated at the SAME phase error, so this is a like-for-like comparison. At the sqrt(3*lambda*L) flare the corrugated horn is actually slightly BEHIND on raw gain - its J0 taper is heavier than the TE11 one. The reason to corrugate is pattern symmetry and cross-polarisation, not gain.

validity: balanced hybrid HE11 assumed, which needs quarter-wave corrugations and several of them per wavelength; a shallow or coarse corrugation does not produce it
aperture-field model with quadratic phase, as for the smooth horn
efficiency fit covers s in [0, 0.8]
the cross-polarisation figure is indicative and not computed

known_cases.source: Near the uniform-phase limit: a 0.1 flare leaves only 0.00375 wavelengths of edge phase error, where the efficiency is 0.691640 against the zero-phase value 0.691660 - the 0.69 quoted in the literature. A vanishing flare would test the limit more exactly but would describe a horn a fraction of a millimetre across, so this stops at a small aperture that is still a real antenna.
At the sqrt(3*lambda*L) flare the HE11 efficiency falls to 0.51734, against the smooth horn's 0.53847 at the same phase error.
quarter-wave corrugations, 7.495 mm at 10 GHz

archetypes.name: Open-ended rectangular waveguide
archetypes.summary: Unflared waveguide aperture; the low-gain limit of the horn family.

analysis.notes: exactly 8/pi^2 = 0.8106 for the TE10 cosine distribution across a, uniform across b
ignores the aperture mismatch, which is significant for an unflared guide
TE10 guide wavelength; diverges at cutoff

validity: single-mode TE10 operation: f0 between the TE10 and TE20 cutoffs
aperture reflection is neglected, so the gain figure is optimistic by a few tenths of a dB
an infinite ground plane is assumed; a bare guide end radiates backward as well

known_cases.source: WR-90 (22.86 x 10.16 mm) at 10 GHz: TE10 cutoff = c/(2a) = 6.556 GHz; aperture is only 0.76 x 0.34 lambda, so G = (8/pi^2)*4*pi*A/lambda^2 = 4.20 dBi. Published ~6 dBi figures for open-ended guide usually include a flange. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13

archetypes.name: Diagonal horn
archetypes.summary: Square aperture carrying two orthogonal modes in phase, radiating a symmetric beam polarised along the diagonal.

analysis.notes: DERIVED, not tabulated: for E = y*cos(pi*x/a) + x*cos(pi*y/a), the co-polar aperture efficiency along the diagonal works out to exactly 8/pi^2 = 0.8106. A separable cos*cos aperture would give only 64/pi^4 = 0.657, so the diagonal horn is genuinely more efficient than a pyramidal one.
uniform phase across the aperture, i.e. an infinitely long horn
Quadratic phase error at the centre of each aperture edge, (a/2)^2/(2R) in wavelengths; at the corners it is twice this. The efficiency, beam and cross-polar figures below take it as their input.
R >= a^2/lambda holds the phase error to an eighth of a wavelength at the edge centres - and a QUARTER at the corners, which this note used to call an eighth.

EXACT, in Fresnel integrals: the field y cos(pi x/a) + x cos(pi y/a) under the same quadratic phase in both directions separates, and its co-polar efficiency is the E-plane sectoral horn's phase factor times the H-plane sectoral horn's efficiency at the same edge error - 8/pi^2 with none. otahub.num.horn_pattern's 2-D integration agrees to 1e-6. 0.787 at the example's 0.075, 0.584 at 1/4.
The gain this horn has at its length; gain_ideal_dbi is the infinitely long horn's.

archetypes.name: Dual-mode (Potter) conical horn
archetypes.summary: A step in a conical horn launches TM11 alongside TE11, cancelling the aperture's cross-polar field over a narrow band.

parameters.name: TM11 share of the aperture power
parameters.description: Fraction of the power at the aperture carried by TM11, in phase with TE11 there. The step sets it and is not solved here; everything the aperture does follows from it.

synthesis.notes: optimum-gain conical relation, the same one the smooth and corrugated horns in this family use

INDICATIVE. The step must sit where TE11 propagates and TM11 is just above cutoff - TM11 cuts off at d = 1.22*lambda in a circular guide, so a diameter a little above that is where the mode is launched. The exact diameter and step height set the TM11 fraction and need a mode-matching solve.

analysis.notes: DERIVED, exact for the aperture: TE11 plus TM11 in phase at the aperture, a fraction tm11_fraction of the power in TM11, and the 3/8-wavelength quadratic phase error that dm = sqrt(3 lambda L) puts at the rim. The co-polar integrals and powers of the two modes are four constants here, computed by otahub.num.horn_pattern; the formula reproduces its direct integration to 1e-12. 0.506 at the default 0.15 - against the INDICATIVE 0.62 this spec carried, which sat between the smooth horn at this phase error (0.51) and the corrugated horn at none (0.69), two numbers that were not comparable.

Against the smooth conical horn of the same length and phase error (TE11 alone, 0.53847). NEGATIVE for any useful mode mix: -0.27 dB at the default. The TM11 tapers the E-plane rim, which is what equalises the beams and cancels the cross-polar field - and a tapered aperture has less gain, not more. The +0.85 dB this spec asserted came from the incomparable efficiencies above.

SOLVED by aperture integration (otahub.num.horn_pattern) and fitted as the half-power point U = D sin(theta_h) in sqrt(tm11_fraction) and 1/D^2, D = dm/lambda from 2 to 40 and the fraction up to 0.4: 0.0014% worst on 136 patterns, 0.0012% on 5 held out. NaN outside that. The TM11 tapers the E plane and broadens its beam: 64.2 lambda/dm with none, 82.0 at the default.

Same fit (0.0002% worst, 0.0005% held out). The H plane barely moves - 75.8 to 81.6 lambda/dm over the whole range. The two beams are equal at a TM11 fraction of 0.097 (0.098 for a horn 3 wavelengths across), about 78 lambda/dm - not the 68 this spec quoted as 'equal in E and H'. At the default 0.15 the E plane is already 4% wider than the H.

SOLVED: the peak cross-polar level (Ludwig-3) in the 45-degree plane relative to the co-polar peak, from otahub.num.horn_pattern at dm = 3.16, 5.48 and 12 wavelengths over the fraction 0-0.4 (0.0025 steps around the null), interpolated linearly in the fraction and in 1/D^2; eight held-out solutions at 4.2 and 8 wavelengths agree to 0.03 dB. Held at the 12-wavelength values above that (worth about 0.05 dB), NaN below 3.15 wavelengths or past a fraction of 0.4. -17.6 dB with TE11 alone; a null of -34.1 to -34.5 dB near a fraction of 0.13; -32.2 dB at the default - so the INDICATIVE -30 dB this spec carried was about right at the design frequency. Only there: the two modes travel at different speeds, and the phase condition that cancels the cross-polar field drifts off with frequency.
Solved from the two beamwidth fits: E- and H-plane half-power beamwidths coincide at 0.0970 for a large horn, 0.0972 at 5.5 wavelengths, 0.0979 at 3.

Solved: where the peak cross-polar level is lowest - 0.1275 at 12 wavelengths across, 0.130 at 5.5, 0.1325 at 3.2 (resolved to 0.0025). Not the equal-beam mix: the two design goals pull a third apart, and a horn tuned for one gives up about 3 dB of cross-polar null or 4% of beam balance for the other.
TM11 cuts off where k*a equals the first zero of J1, 3.8317, i.e. d = 1.2197*lambda. Below this diameter the second mode cannot exist and the horn is simply a smooth one.
TE11 cuts off at the first zero of J1', 1.8412, giving d = 0.5861*lambda

INDICATIVE. The cross-polar cancellation is a phase condition between two modes with different dispersion, so it holds over a few percent. Corrugated horns achieve the same symmetry over an octave, which is why they displaced this design for wideband feeds.

validity: aperture efficiency, beamwidths and cross-polar level are DERIVED from the aperture fields for a given TM11 fraction, at the design frequency; the step that sets that fraction is NOT solved (it needs mode matching), so the fraction is an input, not a result
the aperture phase error is the 3/8 wavelength that dm = sqrt(3 lambda L) implies
narrowband by construction: the mode phase relationship holds at one frequency, and the bandwidth figure remains indicative
the two cutoff diameters are exact, being Bessel zeros

known_cases.source: Exact circular-waveguide cutoffs from the Bessel zeros: TM11 at j(1,1) = 3.8317 gives d = 1.2197*lambda, TE11 at j'(1,1) = 1.8412 gives d = 0.5861*lambda. At 10 GHz, 36.57 mm and 17.57 mm. Cross-checked against this toolkit's circular waveguide module.
sqrt(3*lambda*L) = 164.26 mm for a 300 mm horn at 10 GHz, identical to the smooth conical horn of the same length.

Aperture integration solved directly (otahub.num.horn_pattern) for TE11 + TM11 with 0.15 of the power in TM11, dm = 5.479 wavelengths, 3/8 phase error: efficiency 0.5062, beamwidths 14.970 (E) and 14.352 (H) degrees, peak cross-polar -32.21 dB.

Efficiency 0.50621 solved above against the smooth horn's 0.53847 at the same phase error: a LOSS of 0.27 dB, not the +0.85 dB asserted before. Near zero, so an absolute tolerance, in its own case.
